narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 72.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low academic rankings in law school were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 35 was the third most important factor. While this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still nudged the prediction a bit further toward failure rather than success.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA of 3.20, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class ranking through stronger academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to boost your score. These two steps would most directly address the factors that led to your rejection. (218 words)
